title: Are Phone-Free Schools Working?
author: Carmen Lim, Zach Rausch, Emma Park, and Jon Haidt
summary: Writing for After Babel, Carmen Lim, Zach Rausch, Emma Park, and Jon Haidt summarize a new NYU Stern Tech and Society Lab working paper reviewing seven natural experiments on school phone restrictions. They open with the PISA 2025 results, which show the lowest OECD performance on record and a decline that began in the mid-2010s, and argue that the timing and nature of the drop make the mass migration of childhood onto digital devices a plausible contributor. The core move is to push back against headlines claiming that phone-free schools have 'close to zero impact' on test scores: the authors show that the widely cited Allcott study pooled middle and high schools, masking modest math gains in high schools where phone use was higher and actually fell. They then foreground two less-publicized 2026 studies, Abrahamsson in Norway (benefits for girls, especially lower-income girls) and Lichand in Rio de Janeiro (gains only once bans went school-wide). Finally they argue that test scores are too narrow an outcome, noting that disciplinary incidents rose in year one and then fell, and propose broader measures such as social interaction, library checkouts, and implementation fidelity checks, alongside a living collaborative review of the evidence.
points: The Allcott study's 'close to zero impact' headline pooled middle and high schools; disaggregated, high schools showed modest math gains of roughly one to two months of schooling where phone use was heavier and actually declined.
Among seven natural experiments with similar designs, the middle-school math result in Allcott is the only harmful effect found; most studies show beneficial or neutral effects.
Rio de Janeiro's staged rollout suggests classroom-only bans barely moved scores, while school-wide bans produced gains equal to about one-fifth of a year's learning.
Disciplinary incidents rose during the first year of phone bans but returned to baseline or declined by years two and three, a reminder that effects can change over time as norms settle.

The authors urge every study to include an implementation fidelity check and to track whether students simply shift from phones to school laptops, along with social, reading, and well-being outcomes beyond test scores.
quotes: While none of this proves that digital technologies caused the decline in academic performance, the timing, scale and nature of these changes make them plausible culprits.

In short, the studies primarily found either beneficial effects or neutral effects, with few negative effects. The effects on test scores were particularly promising (contrary to recent headlines), especially in cases where phone use actually declined in schools.

In other words, the study found evidence of benefit in high schools (where we know there was a larger problem and we know that phone use dropped) but the overall effect disproportionately reflected results from middle schools (where the problem was smaller and the remedy — phone use reduction — was applied in a lower dose).

They found that the classroom-only ban barely made a difference. It was only once the ban went school-wide that students performed relatively better on their Math and Portuguese tests, compared to students who were not affected by the ban.

Two studies examined disciplinary incidents, and both found that disciplinary incidents increased during the first year of implementation for middle and high schools. At first glance, that sounds like evidence that the policies backfired. But, in both studies, the trend reversed after the first year.

If the policy is poorly designed or poorly enforced such that phone use does not actually decline, then there is no reason to expect other outcome variables to show any benefits. It is also vital to measure usage of school-provided laptops to find out whether students are simply switching from their phones to their laptops to watch TikTok and play video games during the school day.

Test scores and general well-being cannot tell us whether students are talking to one another more, moving around more, forming stronger friendships and reading more books, or whether teachers find their classrooms easier to manage.
